units.title: Owner or lender?
units.blurb: Ownership, debt, and the two main kinds of shares.

units.title: How funds trade and invest
units.blurb: Trading structure and investment strategy are different dimensions. Fund terminology follows common US usage.

units.title: What does the fund hold?
units.blurb: Equity, debt, and short-term cash management.

units.title: Value, price, and costs
units.blurb: Separate what assets are worth, what you pay, and how fees are charged.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: owning 10 of a company's 1,000 shares gives you a 1% stake.
learning.application: Identify whether a product gives you ownership or a claim for repayment.
learning.misconception: Share ownership does not guarantee dividends or recovery of the purchase price.

concepts.caption: A slice of ownership in a business.
concepts.definition: A security representing company ownership, with business and price risk and possible dividends or capital gains.
concepts.example: Buying this stock makes you a part-owner, not a lender to the company.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Stock means ownership; a bond is debt. Neither dividends nor repayment is risk-free. Share is a common ownership-unit expression, not another product here.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: a 1,000-face-value bond with a 3% annual coupon promises 30 a year. That coupon is not necessarily your purchase yield.
learning.application: Read the issuer and repayment terms, and distinguish face value from the trading price.
learning.misconception: A maturity date does not prevent default or a loss on an earlier sale.

concepts.caption: Lend to an issuer under agreed repayment terms.
concepts.definition: A debt security with contractual payment terms, exposed to default and market-price risk.
concepts.example: The bond promises repayment at maturity rather than ownership of the issuer.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Bondholders lend; stockholders own. A payment obligation is not a risk-free guarantee.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: after creditors and preferred claims are satisfied, common shareholders divide what remains, possibly nothing.
learning.application: Check voting rights, distribution terms, and liquidation priority for the share class.
learning.misconception: A vote is not a guarantee of income or control.

concepts.caption: Usually carries votes, but ranks behind preferred shares in liquidation.
concepts.definition: Ordinary ownership, usually with voting rights and discretionary dividends; residual claims rank behind creditors and preferred shareholders.
concepts.example: Common stock holders voted at the meeting but received no dividend this year.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Common stock usually carries votes; preferred stock usually has distribution priority. Read the issue terms.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: available assets pay creditors, then preferred claims under their terms, then common shareholders.
learning.application: Read dividend deferral, redemption, and conversion provisions.
learning.misconception: Priority is not deposit protection or a capital guarantee.

concepts.caption: Usually has distribution priority, while remaining equity.
concepts.definition: Shares generally ranking ahead of common equity for dividends and liquidation, often with limited voting rights; terms vary.
concepts.example: Preferred stock ranks ahead of common shares for the stated distributions.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Preferred means priority over common equity, not over creditors and not protection from loss.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: an applicable next NAV of 10 buys 100 shares for 1,000 before fees.
learning.application: Check order cutoffs, valuation rules, and charges. Other jurisdictions and products can differ.
learning.misconception: Mutual fund does not mean actively managed, nor every public fund in every country.

concepts.caption: Usually bought or redeemed at the next calculated NAV.
concepts.definition: In common US open-end usage, a pooled fund whose investor orders generally use the next calculated per-share NAV, with applicable fees.
concepts.example: The mutual fund processed the order using its next calculated per-share NAV.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Mutual funds generally use the next NAV; ETFs trade on an exchange at market prices. Either can use active or index strategies.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: a 10.10 purchase price against a NAV of 10 is a 1% premium.
learning.application: Check the price versus NAV, trading spread, and underlying holdings.
learning.misconception: An ETF label alone promises neither indexing nor broad diversification.

concepts.caption: Fund shares bought and sold on an exchange.
concepts.definition: A fund with exchange-traded shares. Market prices can differ from per-share NAV; strategies may be indexed or active.
concepts.example: The ETF traded at 10.10 while its reported per-share NAV was 10.00.
concepts.mixUpWhy: ETF describes the trading structure; index fund describes the strategy. Not every ETF tracks an index or is broadly diversified.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: the index rises 5% and the fund rises 4.7%. Tracking is an objective, not an exact-return promise.
learning.application: Identify the index, its holdings rules, fund costs, and tracking differences.
learning.misconception: An index can fall or concentrate on one narrow industry.

concepts.caption: Seeks to follow an index rather than pick winners.
concepts.definition: A fund seeking to track a market index, through an ETF or mutual-fund structure, subject to costs and tracking differences.
concepts.example: The index fund sought to follow the benchmark rather than beat it through stock picking.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Index funds follow index rules; active funds rely on manager decisions. Exchange trading is a separate distinction.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: a manager cuts a sector before it rallies, leaving the fund behind its benchmark.
learning.application: Compare objectives, holdings changes, and costs against a relevant benchmark.
learning.misconception: Manager discretion does not guarantee outperformance; an ETF can also be active.

concepts.caption: A manager chooses investments rather than simply following index rules.
concepts.definition: A fund whose manager selects or adjusts holdings toward an investment objective; it may be a mutual fund or ETF and can lag its benchmark.
concepts.example: The actively managed fund changed its holdings after the manager revised her outlook.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Active describes manager discretion; index describes rules-based tracking. Mutual fund versus ETF is a different axis.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: 80% shares and 20% cash still leaves a fund mainly exposed to its equity holdings.
learning.application: Read sector, country, and position concentration, separately from fund structure.
learning.misconception: Many holdings in one industry may still be concentrated.

concepts.caption: A fund investing primarily in company shares.
concepts.definition: A fund mainly holding equities, in various structures and strategies, with risk depending on holdings and concentration.
concepts.example: The stock fund held shares in eighty companies rather than lending to those companies.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Stock funds mainly own equity; bond funds mainly hold debt. Both can lose money.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: holdings fall in market value from 100 to 97. All else equal, fund net assets fall too.
learning.application: Check duration, credit quality, and fees to understand the main exposures.
learning.misconception: An ordinary bond fund generally does not promise you repayment on a single maturity date. Product structures vary.

concepts.caption: A debt portfolio whose share value can still move.
concepts.definition: A fund mainly holding bonds or other debt, exposed to interest-rate and credit risk; a fund share is not a single bond with promised maturity payments.
concepts.example: The bond fund lost value when rising rates pushed down the prices of its holdings.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Bond funds mainly hold debt; stock funds mainly hold equity. A bond fund is not a capital guarantee.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: falling short-term rates mean maturing holdings are replaced at lower yields, reducing later income.
learning.application: Check instruments, maturities, liquidity arrangements, and expenses.
learning.misconception: Do not transfer bank-deposit protection rules to fund shares.

concepts.caption: A fund focused on short-term money-market instruments.
concepts.definition: A fund mainly holding short-term debt, cash, or cash equivalents, often for cash management. It is not a bank deposit and can lose money.
concepts.example: The money market fund held short-term instruments instead of a portfolio of long-dated bonds.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Money market funds focus on short-term instruments; bond funds cover a wider maturity and credit range. Low volatility is not a guarantee.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: assets of 1.1 million minus liabilities of 0.1 million, divided by 100,000 shares, give NAV of 10 per share.
learning.application: Compare compatible NAV and trade prices when examining an ETF premium or discount.
learning.misconception: A lower per-share NAV does not make a fund better value or predict higher returns.

concepts.caption: Assets less liabilities; divide again for the per-share value.
concepts.definition: Fund assets minus liabilities give total NAV. Dividing by outstanding shares gives per-share NAV, often shortened to NAV in quotes.
concepts.example: The fund reported NAV of 10 per share, based on net assets divided by shares outstanding.
concepts.mixUpWhy: NAV comes from asset valuation; market price comes from trading. Compare per-share figures with compatible valuation times.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: a price of 9.90 against NAV of 10 is a 1% discount.
learning.application: Check the quote, valuation timing, trading spread, and fees before comparing prices.
learning.misconception: A quoted discount alone is not a guaranteed arbitrage opportunity.

concepts.caption: The price for a fund share in an exchange trade.
concepts.definition: The traded price of an exchange-listed fund share, which can differ from per-share NAV.
concepts.example: The market price was 9.90 per share even though the reported NAV was 10.00.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Market price is what trades; NAV is an asset valuation. An ETF purchase need not occur at NAV.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: a constant 10,000 average holding at 0.5% implies about 50 of annual expenses; actual accrual varies.
learning.application: Separate management costs, total operating expenses, sales charges, and trading costs.
learning.misconception: Do not automatically add a management fee twice or subtract expenses again from returns already net of them.

concepts.caption: Annual operating expenses as a share of average net assets.
concepts.definition: A fund's annual operating-cost percentage, typically including management and other costs; it is neither just the management fee nor every trading cost.
concepts.example: The expense ratio was 0.50% a year, rather than a charge only when shares were bought.
concepts.mixUpWhy: Expense ratio measures ongoing operations; sales load is charged on a purchase or sale. Read them separately.

learning.workedExample: Hypothetical: a 2% front-end load on a 1,000 payment takes 20, leaving 980 invested.
learning.application: Check the fee base, purchase or redemption timing, and waivers. Local terminology and rules can differ.
learning.misconception: No-load funds can still charge operating and other expenses.

concepts.caption: A sales charge on buying or redeeming some fund shares.
concepts.definition: A sales-related purchase or redemption charge used by some funds, distinct from operating expenses and other transaction charges; read the fee table.
concepts.example: A front-end sales load reduced the amount of the payment that was invested.
concepts.mixUpWhy: A load is tied to purchase or redemption; expense ratio covers ongoing operations. No load does not mean no costs.
